newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Conflicts seen stalling Caucasus push to outside world.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Conflicts seen stalling Caucasus push to outside world.

text.p: In more optimistic moments, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan dream of turning their troubled Caucasus region into a new Silk Road, along which vast amounts of goods would travel between Central Asia and Europe.
But Western experts, analysts and diplomats say this idea will stay on paper until the three countries can solve the protracted ethnic conflicts that still divide the region.

It seems the gulf between potential and reality remains frustratingly wide for the three war-weary Caucasus states, keen to bolster their fragile independence by expanding economic ties with the West.
Senior officials from all three countries, making a rare joint appearance at a two-day London conference on the Caucasus late last month, chose at first to be more upbeat.

"There is obvious need for better economic integration. We should aim to create a common economic space stretching from the Black Sea to the Caspian, from the Russian border to the Iranian border," said Georgian parliament chairman Zurab Zhvaniya.
"The traditional role of the region as a crossroads between East and West is becoming a reality.
"Uzbek cotton is transported to Europe through Georgian ports -- this is now the shortest route. We expect to increase shipments of chrome, Siberian aluminium and Kazakh oil."
But before the three states can start working together, they have to overcome some awesome hurdles.

Separatists in Georgia rule over the breakaway territories of South Ossetia and Abkhazia while Armenia and Azerbaijan are deadlocked over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh, inside Azerbaijan but ruled by its Armenian population.

"We're looking mainly at the future when discussing the positive side. The negative is much more with us at present," said Dr Edmund Herzig, senior research fellow and Caucasus specialist at the International Institute of Strategic Studies.
While Armenia and Azerbaijan pay lip service to the idea of closer integration, both accuse the other of using economic levers such as blockades to further their aims.
"The existence and use of these levers does put into question the idea that the three can develop shared economic interests," said Herzig.
TIES WITH WEST LIMITED
Western eyes are focused on the huge oil reserves in the Azeri sector of the Caspian Sea, but otherwise ties are relatively limited and look set to stay that way.

The leaderships in Nagorno-Karabakh, Abkhazia and South Ossetia have strengthened their positions by holding local elections and Caucasus analysts say they are unlikely to give up their dominance in exchange for promises of increased riches.

"These people have clearly viable states, institutions and economic management systems. The only thing they seem to be lacking is the international recognition," said Inna Matveeva of the International Alert non-governmental organisation.

"They see that North Cyprus has been functioning like this for many years and seems to be surviving. Economic hardship has not pushed people to reconciliation. What are the incentives for these societies to make peace?"

Western experts say there are some signs of hope for resolving the Abkhaz and South Ossetian stalemates but are much gloomier about Nagorno-Karabakh, focus of a nine-year fight between Azerbaijan and Armenia.
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union, Armenian troops seized the territory between their border and the enclave and now occupy 20 percent of Azerbaijan.
Both sides are sticking to a locally-agreed ceasefire but show no signs of finding a permanent solution.
During the conference Azeri and Armenian delegates exchanged familiar accusations, showing how much remains to be done.

"We don't trust the Azeris and they don't trust us -- this is the position. We could have solved some problems if we had some trust," conceded Gerard Libaridian, senior adviser to Armenian president Levon Ter-Petrosyan.
Conspiracy theorists in the three republics look over their shoulder towards Russia, widely accused of interfering in the Caucasus to keep the region weak and thereby close to Moscow.

"There are forces which see independent Azerbaijan and Armenia as aberrations, temporary events, so this is why we should work closely together for the benefit of our peoples," said Azeri deputy foreign minister Mahmud Mamed-Kuliyev.
Libaridian seemed to agree, saying Armenia should cooperate with Georgia and Azerbaijan to foster confidence and create the possibility of reaching a conclusive peace.

But in the next breath he ruled out making any more concessions to Azerbaijan to lessen the tension: "Any further steps will strengthen the position of those in Baku who feel the international community can pressurise Armenia into giving in."
